blocks.text: Multi-agent communication goes beyond the general concept introduced in the earlier Multi-Agent Prompting topic to cover the actual mechanics of how messages pass between agents, structured message formats, shared versus private context, and turn-taking order.

This topic covers structuring messages so agents interpret them consistently, what context should be shared between agents versus kept private, managing turn order and one agent waiting on another, and debugging communication failures when agents genuinely miscommunicate.
1. From the General Concept to Actual Mechanics

blocks.alt: Building on multi-step reasoning, multi-agent communication covers the actual message passing mechanics

blocks.text: The earlier Multi-Agent Prompting topic introduced the generator and critic pattern as a general idea, this topic goes deeper into the actual mechanics, how a message from one agent actually gets structured and passed to another so it gets interpreted correctly and consistently.
2. Multi-Agent Prompting vs Communication Mechanics

blocks.alt: Multi-agent prompting is the general concept, multi-agent communication covers how messages actually pass between agents

blocks.text: Where the earlier topic covered why multiple specialized roles can outperform one generalist prompt, this topic covers the practical how, the actual message format, content structure, and passing mechanism that makes that collaboration reliably work in practice.
3. Structuring Messages Between Agents

blocks.alt: An unstructured, freeform message is compared against a structured message with sender, content, and intent

blocks.text: This connects directly to the structured outputs concepts covered in an earlier module, a message from one agent to another benefits from clear structure, who is sending it, what it actually contains, and what it is asking the receiving agent to do, rather than an unstructured block of freeform text the receiving agent has to interpret from scratch.
4. Shared Context vs Private Context

blocks.alt: Shared context is visible to both agents, private context is visible to only one

blocks.text: Not every piece of context needs to be visible to every agent, a critic agent may only need the draft content and the original criteria, not the generator agent full internal reasoning process, deciding what stays shared versus private keeps each agent context focused and avoids unnecessary token overhead, connecting to context window optimization covered in an earlier module.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Context Type","Example"],"rows":[["Shared","The task goal and the current draft under review"],["Private","One agent internal reasoning not relevant to the other"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Turn-Taking and Communication Order

blocks.alt: Agent A speaks, agent B waits its turn, then agent B responds

blocks.text: A multi-agent system needs a clear, defined order for who communicates when, a generator producing a draft before a critic reviews it only works if that sequence is enforced, an undefined or inconsistent turn order risks agents talking past each other or acting on incomplete information.
6. Handling One Agent Waiting on Another

blocks.alt: Agent A waiting on agent B risks no response, triggering a timeout and fallback handling

blocks.text: This connects to the fallback handling concept covered in earlier topics in this module, if an agent expected to respond fails to do so, or produces something unusable, the waiting agent needs an explicit fallback, a retry, a timeout, or an escalation, rather than remaining stuck indefinitely.

blocks.title: This mirrors distributed systems communication concerns
blocks.content: Handling a non-responsive or malfunctioning component gracefully, rather than assuming every communication always succeeds, is a standard concern in any system with multiple communicating parts, multi-agent AI systems are no exception.

blocks.text: 7. A Worked Multi-Agent Communication Example

A generator agent produces a draft and sends it as a structured message to a critic agent, the critic responds with a structured critique message identifying specific issues, the generator receives this critique as input for its next revision, this structured back and forth continues for a fixed number of rounds or until the critic reports no further significant issues.
8. Debugging Multi-Agent Communication Failures

blocks.alt: A communication failure gets logged and inspected for root cause

blocks.text: This connects directly to the prompt debugging techniques covered in an earlier module, when a multi-agent system produces a wrong result, inspecting the actual messages passed between agents, not just the final output, reveals whether the failure came from one agent reasoning, or from a genuine miscommunication, a message misinterpreted or malformed along the way.
9. Multi-Agent Communication and Routing

This connects back to routing prompts, covered earlier in this module, a system routing an incoming request to a specialized assistant, and that assistant then communicating with a second specialized agent, are both instances of the same underlying concern, correctly directing information to the right destination at the right time.
Worked Example

A team building a two agent content review system finds their generator and critic agents occasionally talk past each other, the critic sometimes reviews an outdated draft because messages were not clearly labeled with which version they referred to.

Restructuring messages to include an explicit version identifier alongside the sender, content, and intent resolves this, the critic can now always confirm it is reviewing the current draft rather than an earlier one, eliminating the miscommunication that was previously causing inconsistent review cycles.
Common Mistakes

items: Passing unstructured, freeform messages between agents instead of clearly structured ones with sender, content, and intent
Sharing an agent entire internal context with another agent that only needs a small, relevant portion of it
Not defining a clear turn-taking order, risking agents acting on incomplete or out of sequence information
Having no fallback for when an agent expected to respond fails to do so or produces something unusable

blocks.text: Practice

Design a structured message format for a two agent system you have in mind, generator and critic, or another pairing, specifying sender, content, and intent fields, and define what happens if the receiving agent does not respond as expected.
Key Takeaway

Multi-agent communication requires structured messages with clear sender, content, and intent, a deliberate distinction between shared and private context, an enforced turn-taking order, and explicit fallback handling for non-responsive agents, going beyond the general multi-agent concept into the actual mechanics that make collaboration between agents reliably work.
